analysis.one_liner: Requires the IRS to offer free online tax preparation, filing, and pre-filled return data.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with 11 Senate cosponsors, was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the IRS to build and run free online tax preparation and filing software, let taxpayers download the income information employers and banks already report to the IRS, and pre-fill or fully prepare simple returns for eligible filers at no charge. It also barred the Treasury Department from signing any agreement restricting the IRS's right to offer free filing services, and it moved the deadline for employers and banks to send income reports to January 31 so that data would be ready at the start of tax season.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers who currently pay for commercial tax preparation or spend hours doing their own returns. The bill's free IRS software, downloadable income data, and optional IRS-prepared returns for simple situations (single filers with only wages, interest, or dividends and the standard deduction) would have let millions file at no cost, and the ban on agreements restricting IRS filing services was aimed at keeping a free public option permanently available.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the IRS to establish and operate free online tax preparation and filing software, with no fee allowed for anyone using the program.

Creates a program for taxpayers to download, in printable and computer-readable form, the income information third parties like employers and banks report to the IRS, with the data available within 15 days of receipt so filers are not hunting down forms.

Lets taxpayers with simple situations — unmarried, taking the standard deduction, with income only from wages, interest, or dividends — elect to have the IRS prepare their return for them, with eligibility to expand at the IRS's discretion to married filers, households with dependents, and Earned Income Tax Credit recipients after 2018.

Prohibits the Treasury Secretary from entering into any agreement restricting the government's right to provide tax return preparation or filing services, blocking arrangements that would keep the IRS from competing with paid tax preparation products.

Moves the deadline for information returns (W-2s, bank interest statements and similar forms) to January 31 and eliminates extensions, so the data feeding the download and pre-filled return programs is available before filing season starts.

analysis.who_pays: The IRS and taxpayers generally fund building and running the new free programs, which the bill authorizes through appropriations for fiscal years 2018 through 2022. Employers, banks, and other institutions filing information returns bear earlier deadlines with no extensions. The commercial tax preparation and software industry loses the fees of customers who switch to the free government option.

drawbacks.text: Building and securing the new systems would cost real money; the bill authorizes 'such sums as may be necessary' for fiscal years 2018 through 2022 rather than a fixed amount, leaving the ultimate cost to appropriators.

Putting pre-filled data and return preparation into IRS systems concentrates sensitive financial information in federal systems, and the bill requires identity verification 'to the satisfaction of the Secretary' without specifying the method — a genuine fraud and security concern an honest supporter would acknowledge.

The IRS-prepared return program starts narrow: in its first year only the Secretary would decide which simple-filer populations qualify, and expansion to married couples, dependents, and tax-credit recipients is discretionary, so the hardest-to-file taxpayers would benefit least at first.

Moving information-return deadlines to January 31 with no extensions imposes compliance costs on employers, banks, and payroll processors, some of whom would have less time to correct errors before filers use the data.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are direct and broad: hundreds of millions of Americans file returns every year, and a genuinely free government option with downloaded income data would save filers both money and hours, while the ban on restrictive agreements protects the free option over time. The costs are real but limited — an appropriation to build secure IRS systems, tighter reporting deadlines for employers and banks, and lost revenue for tax-preparation companies. The design is careful about security and taxpayer responsibility, though the initial eligibility for IRS-prepared returns is narrow and expansion depends on the executive branch's discretion. On balance the bill's costs are modest against its reach; its main obstacle was not design but that it never got a hearing.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee in April 2017, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Senator Elizabeth Warren introduced the bill on April 24, 2017, joined by ten cosponsors — nine Democrats and one Independent — and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee the same day.

No further action is recorded: the Finance Committee never held a markup or hearing, the bill never reached the Senate floor, and the congressional record shows no vote of any kind before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

The bill died with no floor vote even though the free-filing idea it embodied continued to be debated publicly in later years, including scrutiny of the IRS's agreements with private tax-preparation companies.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Commercial tax preparation and software companies are better off because the bill died: no free IRS filing competitor was built, no ban on restrictive IRS agreements was enacted, and taxpayers continued to pay for commercial preparation and filing. The Senate Finance Committee's inaction, with no hearing or vote, produced that result.

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled the cosponsor group.

for.name: 10 of 46 Senate Democrats
for.role: Cosponsors (Sens. Shaheen, Baldwin, Franken, Udall, Whitehouse, Markey, Leahy, Duckworth, Hassan), plus 1 Independent (Sen. Sanders)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on.

against.name: Orrin Hatch
against.what_they_did: The committee he chaired received the bill on referral and never scheduled a hearing or markup; it sat with no action for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Tax preparation and software industry (Intuit, H&R Block and similar companies)
against.what_they_did: The industry has long lobbied against government-run free tax filing and in favor of keeping the private Free File arrangement with the IRS, which the bill's prohibition on restrictive agreements was written to override.

sides.party_line_note: All 10 Democratic senators and 1 Independent who signed on were the only cosponsors; no Senate Republican cosponsored, and the Republican-chaired Finance Committee never acted on it.

industries.industry: Tax preparation and software companies (Intuit, H&R Block, Liberty Tax)
industries.note: A free IRS preparation, data-download, and filing program would compete directly with paid products and with the private Free File arrangement, and the bill explicitly barred agreements restricting the IRS from offering these services. The industry's interest runs against the bill's core purpose of letting people file for free.

They would face a hard January 31 deadline for information returns with no extensions, a real compliance cost, but their wage and interest data would feed the download and pre-filled-return programs that make filing easier for their employees and customers.
